overview: Rome’s republic emerged around 509 BCE, although its earliest story comes mostly from much later writers. By the third century BCE it governed peninsular Italy, and then expanded around the Mediterranean. Citizens argued over offices and power while conquered peoples and enslaved workers experienced that expansion very differently. The map interleaves “Rome” (500 to 100 BCE) and “Roman Republic” (400 to 1 BCE). These are coverage labels, not separate states or precise lifespans.

periods.title: A beginning remembered later
periods.summary: Roman tradition places the new republic around 509 BCE. Early written histories were composed centuries afterward, so the details of its first institutions need caution. This phase overlaps the Rome label and precedes the Roman Republic label.

periods.title: Citizens contest political power
periods.summary: Office and voting rights changed during conflicts among Roman citizens. By 287 BCE wealthy plebeians had gained political standing beside patricians; this did not make all residents equal.

periods.title: Power across Italy
periods.summary: By 264 BCE Rome had taken control of peninsular Italy and was about to send armies into Sicily. Roads such as the Via Appia, begun in 312 BCE, helped connect the growing state.

periods.title: A Mediterranean power
periods.summary: War and diplomacy brought territories beyond Italy under Roman control. Provincial rule made Rome powerful while concentrating gains and burdens unequally.

periods.title: Civil conflict and Caesar
periods.summary: Competition over land, wealth and command destabilized republican politics. Julius Caesar became dictator and was assassinated in 44 BCE, but that murder did not restore the old republic.

periods.title: The Augustan settlement
periods.summary: Further conflict followed Caesar’s death. His adopted heir Octavian consolidated power and received the title Augustus in 27 BCE, a conventional marker for the Republic’s political end.

periods.title: People and institutions continue
periods.summary: The imperial regime followed the Republic. Roman communities, roads, languages and many political forms continued. The Rome label ends around 100 BCE and the Roman Republic label around 1 BCE; neither marks the conventional political transition in 27 BCE.

sections.title: A road built for armies, then everyone else

items.text: The Via Appia began in 312 BCE under Appius Claudius Caecus and first linked Rome to Capua. Its straight route served military expansion. As the network grew, it also connected towns, farmland and trade. The present heritage route includes centuries of later construction, so its full length did not spring up in one Republican building season.

UNESCO describes milestones, fountains and stopping places along the Via Appia. A traveler could use the road without paying a toll. That does not mean every journey was pleasant: reaching the next water stop still took real work from people and animals.

The Cloaca Maxima carried drainage from Rome’s Forum area toward the Tiber. The river could also flood that low ground. This large drain was infrastructure for a city built around wet valleys, not evidence that every household had a flushing toilet.

sections.title: A bedroom full of almost-real things

items.text: A villa bedroom painted around 50 to 40 BCE at Boscoreale showed imaginary courtyards, fountains and a glass bowl of fruit. The fruit looked inviting, but it was part of a wall painting. This was an elite home; its vivid walls tell us about one household’s taste, not the décor of every Roman bedroom.

Cato’s second-century BCE farm book gives a recipe for savillum: cheese, flour, honey and an egg baked in a dish, then finished with more honey and poppy seeds. That is a recipe someone wrote down, not proof that every Roman child ate the same dessert. It sounds sticky enough to require a good napkin.

The same book describes a dish it calls “Punic porridge,” made with soaked groats, fresh cheese, honey and egg. The name is Cato’s label; it does not prove exactly how people in Carthage prepared their breakfast.

sections.title: Party cups with a name on them

items.text: A mid-first-century BCE set of silver dining vessels, said to have come from Tivoli, includes cups, a pitcher, a ladle and spoons. Inscriptions on two cups and a ladle record their weight and name Sattia, daughter of Lucius, as owner. Those objects give a woman’s name from a luxury dining set; they do not describe a typical household’s cupboard.

The Metropolitan Museum suggests this silver may have been hidden during late Republican civil unrest. That is possible, but nobody left a note explaining why it was buried. The surviving cups tell us much more securely about dining equipment than about the owner’s last day.

sections.title: School was not the same for every child

items.text: In the late Republic, some families taught young children at home; affluent households could hire a tutor. Other children might attend a teacher for letters, writing and arithmetic. Access depended on family resources, and many children did not receive the same schooling.

A well-off child might be accompanied by an enslaved pedagogue who kept track of lessons and sometimes helped teach. That is a reminder that skill and knowledge existed among people denied freedom. A wealthy pupil could get help with homework from someone who had far fewer choices.

A Roman terracotta model of a breast, dated broadly to the third through first centuries BCE, was dedicated at a healing shrine. A person could offer a body-part model when seeking help from a god. The object does not tell us who made the offering, what illness they faced, or whether they recovered.

sections.title: A tiny piece of real Latin

items.text: A gold coin minted in Rome in 46 BCE carries C·CAESAR COS·TER in the Roman alphabet. The abbreviated Latin means “Gaius Caesar, consul for the third time.” The letters advertise a politician’s office on a portable object. This is one surviving inscription, not a sign that everyone could read or afford a gold coin.

ending.text: The Republic did not end in a single assassination. Caesar was killed in 44 BCE; civil conflict continued, and Octavian received the title Augustus in 27 BCE after consolidating power. The political system changed into an imperial regime, while Roman people and much of their built and cultural world continued. The map labels end around 100 BCE (Rome) and 1 BCE (Roman Republic), on either side of that political transition.
